title: Griffiths phase in clique percolation in random geometric graphs
authors: Vasilii Tiselko, Olga Valba, Alexander Gorsky
abstract: In this study, we discuss the clique percolation in the ensembles of random geometric graphs with different kernels that quantify the geometrical constraints. For the sharp cut-off we find the wide Griffiths phase of extended criticality with the power-law behavior. One boundary of the Griffiths phase is the generalization of a percolation critical point for the ER ensemble when the percolation within the large but finite cluster emerges. The second boundary corresponds to the point in the parameter space when the percolation in the entire clustered system becomes available. For the power-law kernel, richer behavior with a clique-size-dependent boundary between the effective ER and geometric regimes has been identified. The Griffiths phase in this case exists as well. Finally, the pattern with the exponential kernel has been analyzed. We briefly discuss the possible applications of our findings.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes $k$-clique percolation in Random Geometric Graphs, identifying a Griffiths phase characterized by extended criticality. The authors develop sophisticated statistical tools to distinguish between local branching thresholds and global cluster formation thresholds. This work provides deep insights into how geometric constraints modify standard percolation theory in disordered media.
main_problem: The study characterizes the Griffiths phase of extended criticality arising from clique percolation within random geometric graphs (RGGs). It distinguishes between local continuation criticalities and global cluster formation criticalities.
main_result: The analysis identifies two distinct boundaries defining the Griffiths phase, particularly for power-law kernels. The relevant transition point is governed by the peak of the finite-component susceptibility ($\chi_{	ext{finite}}$), which accounts for spatial localization effects absent in simpler models like ER graphs.
method: The authors use advanced statistical mechanics techniques involving size-biased excess completion intensities ($\Lambda_k$) and component-count laws to derive exact formulas for susceptibilities. They compare local branching criteria ($B_k=1$) with global coalescence criteria ($\max E[\chi_{	ext{finite}}(q)]$).
model_or_system: The model is clique percolation on Random Geometric Graphs $G(q)$ defined on a d-dimensional domain using various radial connection kernels (sharp cut-off, power-law, exponential). The focus is on the formation and connectivity of $k$-cliques.
key_observables: k-clique percolation threshold; Griffiths phase behavior (power-law); finite-component susceptibility ($\chi_{	ext{finite}}(q)$); local continuation factor ($B_k$).
important_parameters: Kernel type (e.g., power-law, exponential); dimensionality $d$; clique size $k$; critical parameter $\eta = \alpha/d$.
main_assumptions: The analysis often employs a 'one-large closure' ($\chi_{\ell}^{finite}$) when exact tail probabilities are intractable, approximating the contribution of the largest component. The local onset is modeled using a branching skeleton approach.
figures_summary: Not specified in notes; the structure suggests comparisons between different critical points derived from various mathematical criteria (e.g., $\chi_{all}$ vs $\chi_{	ext{finite}}$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing local criticality via branching processes, then introduces global cluster dynamics using component-count laws to define a finite-component susceptibility ($\chi_{	ext{finite}}$). Finally, it analyzes the scaling behavior of this susceptibility across different kernel regimes and dimensions.
why_interesting: While focused on graph theory/percolation, the methodology—using moment calculations (second moment $\chi$) to pinpoint phase transitions in systems with quenched disorder or geometric constraints—is highly relevant for understanding localization phenomena in disordered quantum systems or spin glasses.
